description: Hooke's law for springs, elastic and plastic deformation, elastic potential energy, moments, levers and gears.
content_html:
Elastic and Plastic Deformation

To stretch, bend or compress an object, more than one force must be applied. A single force would simply cause the object to accelerate (Newton’s Second Law). Two opposing forces are required for deformation — for example, a weight pulling a spring downwards while the support holds it up.

When forces are applied to a spring, it can undergo two types of deformation:

• Elastic deformation — the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed. The spring ‘bounces back.’
• Plastic deformation — the object is permanently deformed. The spring has been stretched beyond its elastic limit and does not recover.

Hooke’s Law

Hooke’s Law states that the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, as long as the elastic limit is not exceeded. The equation is:

$$F = k \times e$$

Where \(F\) is force (N), \(k\) is the spring constant (N/m), and \(e\) is extension (m). Extension is the change in length: \(e = \text{stretched length} - \text{natural length}\). A larger spring constant means a stiffer spring. On a force-extension graph, the straight-line region confirms Hooke’s Law; the gradient of this line equals the spring constant \(k\). Beyond the elastic limit, the graph curves — deformation becomes plastic.

Key Fact

Hooke’s Law: \(F = ke\). The gradient of the straight-line section of a force-extension graph equals the spring constant \(k\). Beyond the elastic limit, deformation is plastic and permanent.

Clamp a spring vertically from a stand. Measure and record the natural length using a ruler. Add known masses one at a time, recording the total length each time. Calculate extension for each mass (\(e = \text{new length} - \text{natural length}\)). Plot force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis). The straight-line section confirms Hooke’s Law; the point where the line begins to curve marks the elastic limit. To improve accuracy, take repeated readings at each force and calculate the mean; read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax; ensure the spring hangs freely without touching the stand.

When a spring is stretched elastically, energy is stored as elastic potential energy (EPE):

$$E_e = \frac{1}{2} \times k \times e^2$$

Where \(E_e\) is elastic potential energy (J), \(k\) is the spring constant (N/m), and \(e\) is extension (m). This equation only applies within the elastic limit (the linear region). On a force-extension graph, the EPE equals the triangular area under the straight-line section: \(\frac{1}{2} \times F \times e\). When the spring is released, this stored energy is transferred to kinetic energy or gravitational potential energy.

Moments

A moment is the turning effect of a force about a pivot. It is calculated using:

$$M = F \times d$$

Where \(M\) is the moment (N m), \(F\) is the force (N), and \(d\) is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (m). The distance must be perpendicular to the force — using a slanted distance gives the wrong answer. Moments are measured in newton-metres (N m).

For an object to be in rotational equilibrium, the total clockwise moment about any pivot must equal the total anticlockwise moment about the same pivot. This is the principle of moments:

$$\text{total clockwise moment} = \text{total anticlockwise moment}$$

Question: A see-saw has a pivot at its centre. A child of weight 300 N sits 1.5 m from the pivot on the left. How far from the pivot must a 450 N adult sit on the right to balance the see-saw?

Step 1: Anticlockwise moment (child) = \(300 \times 1.5 = 450 \text{ N m}\).

Step 2: For equilibrium: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment.
\(450 \times d = 450\)
\(d = 450 \div 450 = 1.0 \text{ m}\).

The adult must sit 1.0 m from the pivot. Notice that the heavier person sits closer to the pivot to produce the same moment.

Key Fact

Moment (N m) = Force (N) × perpendicular distance from pivot (m). For equilibrium: total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment (principle of moments). Distance must be perpendicular to the force.

Levers and Gears

A lever uses the principle of moments to act as a force multiplier. By applying a small effort at a large distance from the pivot, you can overcome a larger load closer to the pivot. For example, a crowbar enables a small downward push to lift a large rock. Scissors, tweezers, a bottle opener and a wheelbarrow are all examples of levers in different configurations.

The key idea: the lever multiplies force because moment = force × distance. If the effort arm is longer than the load arm, the effort force needed is smaller than the load force, even though both produce equal moments.

Gears are toothed wheels that mesh together and transmit turning forces. When two gears of different sizes mesh:

• The smaller gear turns faster but with less force (smaller moment).
• The larger gear turns more slowly but with greater force (larger moment).
• The number of teeth on each gear determines the gear ratio — larger gear ÷ smaller gear. A higher gear ratio means a greater increase in force but a reduction in speed.
exam_tip_html: For Hooke’s Law questions, remember: extension is the change in length, not the total stretched length. In moments calculations, the distance must always be perpendicular to the force — a diagram often helps you identify this. For force-extension graph questions, the elastic limit is where the graph first curves away from the straight line; make sure you identify this point clearly. When asked to describe plastic deformation, state that the object “does not return to its original shape when the force is removed” — vague answers like “stretches too far” will not gain marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hooke’s Law: \(F = ke\). Extension is proportional to force up to the elastic limit. Beyond this, deformation is plastic (permanent). The gradient of the force-extension graph’s straight section = spring constant k.
  • Moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot (unit: N m). For rotational equilibrium, total clockwise moments = total anticlockwise moments (principle of moments).
  • Levers act as force multipliers using the principle of moments. Gears transmit turning forces; a larger gear turns slower but produces a greater turning effect.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following describes elastic deformation?
A) The object is permanently changed in shape
B) The object returns to its original shape when the force is removed
C) The object stretches beyond its elastic limit
D) The object compresses without any force applied
practice_questions.marks: B) The object returns to its original shape when the force is removed [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the equation that links moment, force and distance.
practice_questions.marks:
Moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot [1 mark]
(Accept M = Fd where d is perpendicular distance)

practice_questions.text:
A spring has a natural length of 12.0 cm. When a force of 6.0 N is applied, it stretches to 18.0 cm.
Calculate the spring constant of the spring. Give your answer in N/m.
practice_questions.marks:
Extension = 18.0 − 12.0 = 6.0 cm = 0.06 m [1 mark]
Apply F = ke: k = F ÷ e [1 mark]
k = 6.0 ÷ 0.06 = 100 N/m [1 mark]
Unit: N/m [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would use a spring, masses and a ruler to investigate Hooke's Law in the school laboratory. Include how you would ensure accuracy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes adding masses one at a time, measuring extension each time (not total length), plotting force vs extension, identifying the straight-line region. Mentions parallax-free reading at eye level or repeated readings for accuracy. [2 marks]
Secure: Basic method described but accuracy improvement missing. [1 mark]
Developing: Vague — 'add weights and measure the spring'. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A lever is used to lift a rock. The rock (load) weighs 900 N and is placed 0.4 m from the pivot. An effort force is applied 1.8 m from the pivot on the other side.
Calculate the effort force needed to balance the rock. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Anticlockwise moment (load) = 900 × 0.4 = 360 N m [1 mark]
For equilibrium: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment [1 mark]
Effort × 1.8 = 360 [1 mark]
Effort = 360 ÷ 1.8 = 200 N [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how gears can be used to increase the turning force (moment) of a bicycle's pedalling motion. Include the role of gear size in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that a smaller front gear (chainring) meshes with a larger rear gear (sprocket). The larger rear gear turns more slowly but with a greater turning effect (torque/moment). This is because moment = force × distance — a larger gear has a larger effective radius. Links to gear ratio: larger gear ÷ smaller gear. Applies to practical situation: riding up a hill requires a high gear ratio for more force; riding on flat at speed requires a lower gear ratio. [5–6 marks]
Secure: Correctly explains that a larger gear produces greater force but turns more slowly, with some reference to gear ratio. [3–4 marks]
Developing: States that gears change speed or force, but lacks explanation linking to moments. [1–2 marks]
Emerging: Minimal physics content. [0 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the spring constant k in Hooke's Law equation F = ke?
options: The total force applied to the spring
A measure of the stiffness of the spring, in N/m
The extension of the spring beyond its elastic limit
The maximum force a spring can support

knowledge_checks.q: A 10 N force is applied 0.5 m from a pivot. What is the moment of this force?
Beyond the elastic limit, a spring undergoes _____ deformation and does not return to its original length.
For an object in rotational equilibrium, the total clockwise moment equals the total _____ moment.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Reversible change — object returns to original shape
Turning effect of a force about a pivot (N m)

flashcard_questions.q: State Hooke's Law as an equation.
What is the spring constant k?
flashcard_questions.a: A measure of spring stiffness — force per unit extension, in N/m.
The maximum force beyond which a spring no longer returns to its original length.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the gradient of the straight-line section of a force-extension graph represent?

flashcard_questions.a: Energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object within its elastic limit.

flashcard_questions.q: What equation gives the moment of a force?
flashcard_questions.a: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot (M = Fd), in N m.
For equilibrium, total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment about any pivot.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a lever act as a force multiplier?
flashcard_questions.a: Effort applied far from pivot produces equal moment to a larger load closer to pivot.

flashcard_questions.q: When two gears of different sizes mesh, what does the larger gear do compared to the smaller?
flashcard_questions.a: Turns more slowly but produces a greater turning force (moment).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between elastic and plastic deformation?
flashcard_questions.a: Elastic is reversible; plastic is permanent — object does not return to original shape.

glossary_terms.definition: Deformation that is reversible — the object returns to its original shape and size when the force is removed.
Deformation that is permanent — the object does not return to its original shape when the force is removed.
The extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.
The maximum force that can be applied to a spring before it no longer returns to its original length. Beyond this point, the relationship between force and extension is no longer linear.
A measure of how stiff a spring is, equal to the force per unit extension, measured in N/m.
The energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object, equal to the area under the force-extension graph.
The turning effect of a force about a pivot, equal to force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot. Measured in newton-metres (N m).
The principle that an object in equilibrium has equal total clockwise and anticlockwise moments about any pivot.
A rigid bar that turns about a pivot. Levers allow a small force applied at a large distance from the pivot to produce a large force closer to the pivot.
Toothed wheels that mesh together to transmit and change turning forces. Gears can change the speed and turning effect (torque) of a rotating system.
